satellite-siting.story: You have 24 orbital slots on the table and a launch budget that pays for 9 of them. Each satellite covers a strip of ground on its own, and two well placed satellites cover more between them than either does alone. Filling the nine best looking slots one at a time leaves gaps that a different nine would have closed.

school-places.story: You have 600 applicants and 480 places across 15 schools, with about 3,200 acceptable pairings between them. You want to seat as many applicants as possible somewhere both sides find acceptable. It is hard because the popular places are named by hundreds of applicants at once, so every seat you fill closes off options for someone else, and the best overall result rarely comes from serving the longest queue first.

Each position watches a fixed patch of ground, and two positions whose views meet also cover the strip between them. The widest single views can still leave blind ground that a cheaper pair would have watched. You can think of guards on patrol posts here just as well as sensors.

shift-assignment.story: You have 40 people and 12 shifts to cover, with 96 possible pairings between them, because each person can work some of the shifts and not others. You want to fill as many shifts as you can, one person to a shift. The catch is that an obvious pairing made early can leave someone later with no shift they are able to cover, so a full rota may need several earlier choices undone.

Each location draws its own custom, and two shops close to each other can build up a catchment that neither would hold alone. It is tempting to take the eight busiest streets, though a pair on a quieter street may earn more between them.

Push one point and every point connected to it shifts as well, so the frame answers as a single piece. You want how far each point moves and how hard each member is worked, so you can see which one is closest to its limit.

supply-chain.story: You run 3 factories, 5 depots and 20 shops, joined by 40 shipping lanes with weekly limits. You want the largest amount that can reach the shops in a week, and the one lane that stops it going higher. What makes it awkward is that adding capacity in the wrong place buys you nothing at all: only the lanes that are already full hold the total down.

trading-group.story: You deal with 80 parties and have 950 existing relationships on file. You are looking for the largest circle of parties in which every pair already trades with each other, so nothing fresh has to be negotiated. It is hard because one absent pair spoils the whole circle, however busy the rest of it is. You can think of clearing banks or of suppliers inside one shared agreement here just as well as trading parties.

weakest-link.story: Your network has 16 places in the network and 28 connections between them, each carrying a known amount. You want to know which few connections, if they failed together, would split the network into two halves that cannot reach each other, and how much capacity that would cost you. It is hard because the weak point is rarely the busiest connection: it is the cheapest set of connections that separates one side from the other, and that set can sit far from where the traffic looks heaviest.
